title: Future Fund digs into Bathla collapse as fire sale kicks off
full_text:
The Future Fund, Australia’s sovereign wealth player, sought assurances its investments in Asian private lender PAG had not been embroiled in the collapse of Sydney home builder Bathla Group.
The $356bn fund is the latest major investor to probe a potential exposure to the wounded home builder, with regulators honing their focus on any contagion risks as market watchers warn the fire sale of Bathla sites is about to begin.
Sources have confirmed the $356bn fund questioned PAG on its lending to Bathla, amid concerns the Future Fund’s cash could be caught up in the $3.4bn collapse.
At its peak Bathla was among the biggest builders of affordable homes in Sydney and NSW, with plans to take its vision national, before it collapsed under a growing load of debts and unpaid suppliers.
Sources said the Future Fund was told none of the money it had allocated from its Private Debs strategy, invested with PAG, was tied up in the collapse.
PAG, one of Hong Kong’s biggest private lenders, has extended to Bathla more than $488.1m in loans, of which more than $335m have been drawn down.
A normally tight-lipped lender, PAG has attempted to play down its exposure to Bathla, with sources attempting to suggest its exposure was only circa $300m, well short of its true commitment.
But PAG now faces a hefty task of finishing several of its Bathla projects, including a sprawling site at Pemulwuy, with the risk it may need to draw down more funds to bankroll the job.
The interest by the Future Fund shows the growing scrutiny of private credit investments by Australia’s superannuation sector, which has piled into the market, as well as the risks when things go wrong.
The Future Fund has also invested in Australian domestic housing, tipping around $20bn into the portfolio. These investments are now exposed to the waning fortunes of the Australian housing market, the same winds that battered Bathla, which was placed in administration three weeks ago.
The Future Fund has more than $23.5bn invested in its credit portfolio. Both the prudential regulator and corporate regulator have probed the potential contagion effect from Bathla’s collapse, the risks posed to investors as well as the broader systemic risks in banking and superannuation.
Last week The Australian revealed the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority had asked the banking and superannuation sectors to disclose their potential exposure to Bathla’s conflagration.
An APRA spokesman said the regulator was attempting to understand how banks, which had negligible exposure to Bathla, were exposed to the private credit lenders behind the developer.
“For superannuation, trustees’ due diligence and investment governance (including valuation) of unlisted and illiquid investments has been a point of ongoing focus for APRA,” he said.
“While APRA-regulated superannuation funds have little direct exposure to Bathla, trustees need to ensure their investment governance is prudent, their valuations applied to investments are appropriate and they act in members’ best interests.” Some of Sydney’s biggest real estate firms have also questioned the valuations of Bathla’s lengthy list of land sites, many of which are now hitting the market.
Several of Bathla’s backers have been warning this risked sparking a fire sale and tumbling values. Some property experts warned that the low value real estate held by Bathla sits outside the remit of traditional institutional size developers.
As such, any carve-up would have to be undertaken by smaller, private and local operators, who often rely on the very private credit funds that have now slammed shut.
Some pointed to the possibility of seeking to marry up incomplete sites with new builders, some of whom are looking to take on work in the wake of Bathla’s collapse.
However, this could be an extended process with property experts predicting that the buyers may be left in limbo on incomplete jobs as finding new buyers builders will be tough as they are unwilling to warrant the quality of Bathla’s troubled work.
Buyers also face difficulty settling if lenders take a hard line on the diminished value of Bathla-related properties, potentially costing them their deposits.
Expectations are rising about a veritable flood of Bathla unit and land sites in various stages being brought to market by a mix of receivers and lenders that have gone mortgagee in possession.
The latter course has been pursued by a series of smaller Bathla lenders, as they take control of land parcels and blocks of incomplete or unsold apartments.
They believe that by moving quickly they will be able to get out ahead of the rush. However, the same exit play being executed by smaller and midsize lenders risks flooding the market with around 40 sites as advisers are inundated with requests for advice.
One expert suggested that there would be an extended period of “price discovery” in which lenders who had assumed their loan-to-value ratio was around 70 per cent could find themselves nursing losses.
Potential buyers are also reluctant to buy now when values could fall further, one adviser noted. They said there was no solution to the carve-up, noting Teneo administrators had to attempt to finish nearly complete apartment projects as well as carve off home and land packages for sale.
